rationale: A wins because it keeps its hands cleaner: three usable, structurally different stories without wandering far past the supplied facts. Its pricing angle, "When the AI does the building, Replit charges for the work, not the seat," slightly overstates usage-based pricing on top of subscriptions, but it is still a real business-model lane. B has the sharpest single angle in "It won't say how often those apps actually work," but then spends that advantage on a speculative security story: "Who’s checking what’s in them?" is a question, not yet a pitch.
gaps_in_A: "When the AI does the building, Replit charges for the work, not the seat" overstates the fact pattern; the update says usage-based pricing sits on top of subscriptions, not that Replit has replaced seat pricing.
A misses the strongest accountability angle as a standalone: reliability is "not disclosed," and that is more than proof texture for angles one and two.

"Replit built its name teaching people to code" is a fair inference from education use, but still stronger than the supplied wording; it needs either company history or education-user data before pitching hard.
gaps_in_B: "a huge, largely non-technical user base" is invented. The update says Replit positions the agent for non-engineers; it does not say Replit’s existing tens of millions of users are largely non-technical.

"Replit's new agent lets non-coders spin up live databases. Who's checking what's in them?" stretches into cybersecurity without a supplied security fact, incident, guardrail failure, or researcher finding.
"The agent provisions live databases for people who...aren't engineers" turns positioning into actual user behavior. That needs evidence before it belongs in an angle set.
Rejecting "Replit's usage-based pricing shows where AI agent costs are headed" as a duplicate is a miss; pricing is a distinct business-model story from broad user/category adoption.
